Yet, it has limited application in diagnosing the functional aspects of insulin degrading enzymes within human tissues due to the presence of other biomarkers. This paper examines potential IHC pitfalls that could misinterpret the activity of insulin degrading enzymes. It details common challenges associated with tissue sampling techniques, including sample preservation, staining conditions, and post-hoc analyses. By highlighting these pitfalls, this study contributes to enhancing the reliability and accuracy of IHC analysis in assessing the enzymatic roles of insulin degrading enzymes in human tissues.
title: Immunohistochemical pitfalls in the demonstration of insulin-degrading enzyme in normal and neoplastic human tissues

text: The purpose of this research is to investigate and refine the application of Euclidean geometry in a more systematic manner towards establishing a rigorous theoretical foundation for the notion of entropies as a generalization of information theory and statistical physics. The paper first explores the geometric structure of entropy and its role within statistical thermodynamics, providing a deeper understanding of how entropy can be understood both theoretically and practically. Subsequently, the work delves into various types of entropic quantities such as Boltzmann's entropy, Shannon's entropy, and Renyi's entropy. These entities represent different aspects of entropy and their relationships among each other have been studied extensively but, despite being foundational, some mathematical properties remain largely unexplored. By systematically applying Euclidean methods to these entropy quantities, we aim to enhance our comprehension of their fundamental behavior and derive new relations that go beyond traditional definitions. Specifically, we explore the connection between entropy and geometry, identifying potential geometric interpretations and connections with concepts in topology and dynamical systems. Overall, the investigation aims to expand our toolkit for studying the intricacies of entropy, thereby facilitating the development of a comprehensive and robust framework for quantifying and analyzing complex systems in various fields including physics, statistics, and computer science.
title: Euclidean analysis of the entropy functional formalism

text: This paper aims to examine Spitzer observations of low-luminosity isolated and low-surface-brightness galaxies using high-resolution images. The study utilizes a combination of photometric and optical imaging techniques, including spectroscopy, to obtain detailed insights into these dwarf objects. The motivation for this research was to provide deeper understanding of the formation and evolution processes within these faint cosmic bodies, particularly focusing on their interaction with dark matter haloes. The authors' methodology involved processing raw data from various telescopes across multiple wavelengths to extract reliable information about the physical properties and stellar populations in low-luminosity galaxies. Results indicate that these galaxies show distinctive signatures related to their lower surface brightness and luminosity levels, which might be due to an interplay between star formation efficiency and gravity confinement within their environments.
title: Spitzer Observations of Low Luminosity Isolated and Low Surface Brightness Galaxies

text: Dileucine, an aromatic amino acid with structural similarity to leucine, exhibits properties similar to both peptides and polypeptides. This study investigates the application of annealing importance sampling (AIS) in estimating thermodynamic properties of dileucine-based organic molecules. Through the analysis of the energy landscape during the annealing process, AIS is employed to determine the probability density function for these molecular systems, offering insights into potential conformations or interactions among the dipeptide's atoms. The effectiveness of this method was verified using simulations of three-dimensional structures, showing high precision in quantifying equilibrium constants and other critical thermodynamic characteristics of the system. Overall, this work represents a novel approach to understanding the thermal behavior and conformational space of organometallic dyes, providing valuable data for materials scientists aiming to optimize doping efficiency in solar cells and other technological applications involving metalloorganic compounds.
title: Annealed importance sampling of dileucine peptide

text: Delta Scutum is a star cluster located in the constellation of Puppis, containing over 80 known pulsars and a large number of low-frequency radio sources. In this study, we employ asteroseismology techniques to investigate the stellar structure and evolution in the open cluster Praesepe. Our work utilizes data from the High Frequency Atmospheric Imaging Spectrograph (HFI) aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), providing precise temperature, density, and rotation information for each pulsar. Additionally, we analyze the radial velocities of stars within the cluster using the Gaia Data Release 9 mission, which allows us to study the rotational motion of nearby stars. These observations enable the detailed analysis of the pulsar population, including their mass, radius, and period variations, as well as the evolution of the cluster itself. By combining various data sets, our findings contribute significantly to our understanding of the interstellar medium and the mechanisms governing these structures in high-energy astrophysical environments.
title: Asteroseismology of delta Scuti stars in open clusters: Praesepe

text: Astronomers have discovered an unprecedented sample of 838 RR Lyrae stars in the LONEOS-I survey, which spans approximately a million years in age. By analyzing these stars, they identified new components in the Galactic stellar halo that were not previously detected. This study contributes to our understanding of galactic structure and evolution, highlighting the potential for identifying more massive star clusters and binary systems.
title: Evidence for Distinct Components of the Galactic Stellar Halo from 838 RR Lyrae Stars Discovered in the LONEOS-I Survey

text: In this study, we investigate internal states of model isotropic granular packings by analyzing the assembling process, geometry, and contact networks within each state. Our investigation employs mathematical modeling and simulations to derive analytical solutions for specific states that exhibit unique features in packing configurations. By examining both microscopic aspects (particle interactions) and macroscopic properties (packaging structures), our findings provide insights into fundamental mechanisms governing the formation and stability of these intricate patterns. These insights have potential applications in various fields such as materials science, environmental studies, and computer graphics, where understanding and predicting packing behavior is crucial for optimization and design. Overall, this research contributes significantly to our knowledge of granular materials through empirical observation and theoretical analysis.
title: Internal states of model isotropic granular packings. I. Assembling process, geometry and contact networks

text: In this study, we investigate the impacts of long-term impedance variations (LZV) and wake patterns of XFEL undulators on current-enhanced Spectroscopy for Augmentation (SASE) schemes. By analyzing simulated XFEL data, we observe how these factors affect the response times and signal-to-noise ratios in SASE experiments. The impact on Zeretkin's (FIR-Z) scheme was particularly notable as LZVs exceeding -40 dBc significantly impaired its performance compared to baseline conditions. Furthermore, we found that the effects of LZVs could be exacerbated during pulse amplification, where such modifications can lead to reduced efficiency due to nonlinear dynamics associated with the undulator's wake. This research underscores the importance of comprehensively characterizing and mitigating LZVs before implementing current-enhanced technologies, as their subtle yet significant impacts can significantly degrade the performance of SASE systems.
title: Longitudinal impedance and wake from XFEL undulators. Impact on current-enhanced SASE schemes

text: On the accuracy of overlapping integrals for Slater-type orbitals: analytical versus recurrence techniques Overlapping integrals have been a cornerstone in quantum chemistry but their assessment is often problematic due to uncertainties related to integration constants. This paper presents a novel approach to evaluating these integrals using analytical and recurrence formulas. By employing these methods, it is possible to improve the precision and reliability of calculations. The study demonstrates that both analytical and recurrence techniques provide comparable levels of agreement, highlighting the advantages of this analytical strategy in assessing overlaps between Slater-type orbitals.
title: On the accurate evaluation of overlap integrals over Slater type orbitals using analytical and recurrence relations

text: In this study, researchers explored how open clusters in the universe contribute to cosmic dark energy and the formation of galaxy clusters through the lens of stellar evolution models. A key finding is that the presence and composition of open cluster remnants significantly shape the growth rate and structure of galaxy clusters, providing insight into the fundamental principles governing the formation and evolution of these massive systems in our cosmos. The analysis involved the application of numerical stellar evolution simulations and parameterization techniques to generate realistic galaxy and cluster models. By incorporating information from both the local universe and the broader halo, it was possible to identify the impact of open cluster remnants on the mass distribution and dynamics of large-scale structure. Additionally, the study delved into the mechanisms underlying the observed trends between the total stellar mass in open cluster remnants and the density of galaxies within them. This investigation helped refine theories about the nature of the early universe's distribution and its eventual role as a driving force for cosmic acceleration toward greater expansion rates. The findings suggest that while individual open cluster remnants do play crucial roles in galactic assembly, they can have an overall significant effect on the overall structure of larger structures such as galaxy clusters. The results highlight the importance of understanding the complex interplay between star formation, gravitational interactions, and density perturbations in galaxy formation processes. Future studies will likely explore further the specific scenarios where different types of open cluster remnants dominate or influence galaxy evolution.
title: Characterization of open cluster remnants

text: In recent years, there has been significant interest in exploring the phenomenon of massive planet migration, which is thought to occur at high rates due to the existence of multiple star systems within our galaxy. This astronomical event involves the rapid transfer of planets across stellar systems, often disrupting the orbits of existing terrestrial bodies through tidal forces and gravitational interactions. While theoretical models have provided some insight into the conditions that promote this migration, direct observational evidence remains limited. To address this gap, this research examines both theoretical predictions and data from various observations across different types of planetary systems to provide a comprehensive understanding of planet migrations. Theoretical predictions serve as the foundational basis for any attempt to predict or explain phenomena such as massive planet migration. These predictions generally aim to describe the conditions necessary for mass transfer to take place and how it impacts planetary dynamics on Earth's exoplanets. Through mathematical modeling, various scenarios are simulated, revealing insights into the mechanisms involved in planet migration without invoking the need for empirical verification or definitive experiments. By comparing these predictions against observed data from different regions of the sky and among various planetary systems, scientists can validate their assumptions about mass transfers occurring during migration events. On the other hand, several recent studies have explored observational data that has allowed researchers to directly investigate and confirm theories of planet migrations. Exoplanet transit observations offer unique opportunities to observe the presence and characteristics of planets outside of their current habitable zone but also provide insights into how these systems could be perturbed. Similarly, spectroscopic observations of stars orbiting other stars have shown discrepancies between the expected orbital parameters and actual outcomes, leading researchers to hypothesize alternative scenarios that may drive the observed movements. Observational constraints further add a layer of support to theoretical predictions. By examining the positions and motions of known exoplanets alongside newly discovered transiting planets and spectral-type stars, astronomers uncover patterns and correlations not easily detectable using purely theoretical means. Additionally, detailed surveys of distant galaxies and clusters reveal variations in the properties of interstellar gas, which can impact the trajectories of distant planetary systems. While theoretical modeling offers valuable guidance and serves as a foundation, observational data continues to expand our understanding of massive planet migrations beyond what was previously possible. It underscores the importance of continued interdisciplinary collaboration between astrophysicists and astronomers across different fields of study to explore the full spectrum of astronomical phenomena. As the mechanisms behind migration continue to evolve, future work will likely focus on refining theoretical predictions based on new data, expanding observational techniques to identify more precise cases, and potentially uncovering new unexplained phenomena that challenge conventional understandings. These efforts will ultimately contribute to better predictions and better understanding of planet migrations, potentially impacting our view of the universe's most common and dynamic system.
title: Massive planet migration: Theoretical predictions and comparison with observations

text: The paper presents calculations of Landau-Gaussian propagation kernels corresponding to two different gauge group theories: SU(2) and SU(3). Both of these groups were known as Landau-Gaussian states because their propagators exhibited a nonlocal behavior which led to the appearance of long-ranged repulsion. The results show that the propagator for SU(3) is significantly different from those of the other theory, which was previously considered simpler due to its lack of spontaneous symmetry breaking. This difference becomes even more noticeable in higher order infrared singularities, where both theories produce similar IR singularities but exhibit distinct behaviors due to their different dynamics. Additionally, the authors explore the implications of this difference for the structure constants of gauge-invariant observables, showing how the nonlocal nature of the propagators affects their computation.
title: Just how different are SU(2) and SU(3) Landau-gauge propagators in the IR regime?

text: Motivation: This study aims to utilize advanced deep learning techniques such as Akari (AK) and FIS, which are particularly effective for detecting complex features in astronomical images. Method: The paper presents an experimental setup that involves collecting high-resolution sky scans from the European Southern Observatory's Large Reconnaissance Satellite (LRS), using Akari and FIS deep observations. This allows for the extraction of intricate details on the dust distribution within a star formation region known as CFIRB. Results: By applying Akari and FIS algorithms, the study identified significant changes in the dust density structure observed in CFIRB at a spatial resolution of ~8 pixels per degree. These findings suggest the presence of a substantial amount of interstellar material extending from the nebula core into the extended regions surrounding it. Conclusion: The results demonstrate the potential of advanced computational methods in astronomy to enhance our ability to investigate and characterize complex astronomical phenomena. The use of AKARI and FIS for identifying subtle patterns in CFIRB provides valuable insights into understanding the dust environment and providing support for future space observatories planning to focus on this topic. This study is part of a broader initiative aimed at leveraging deep learning for improved analysis and interpretation of astronomical data.
title: Detection of CFIRB with AKARI/FIS Deep Observations

text: A Novel Spacetime Concept for Describing Electronic Motion Within a Helium Atom Motivation The study of electron motion within helium is crucial in understanding atomic structure. However, previous models often assumed that electrons travel along the trajectory defined by classical mechanics, neglecting quantum mechanical effects. This paper introduces a novel spacetime framework to accurately describe these trajectories. Method The authors use the framework provided by Wigner's "quark model" for quarks as the fundamental particles and develop a modified version based on the principles of relativistic quantum mechanics (RQM) for electrons moving inside an isotropic helium crystal. Results The analysis reveals that the classical trajectory model underestimates the actual path taken by electrons due to quantum fluctuations and correlations between quark moments. The modified model exhibits more realistic dynamics, predicting the correct electron path and quantifying the role played by non-relativistic kinetic energy in determining the path taken by electrons over large distances. Conclusion This new framework not only provides a quantitative insight into the behavior of electrons but also offers insights into the nature of matter at its core. The method presented here can serve as a solid theoretical basis for further research in the fields of physics and condensed matter science.
title: A novel spacetime concept for describing electronic motion within a helium atom

text: Title: The Star-Forming Content in the W3 Giant Molecular Cloud Aims: To determine the amount of stellar material composing the core regions of the W3 giant molecular cloud (GC1) at the center. Methology: We use two different radiometer techniques to map the surface temperature distribution of GC1 from its outermost edge to its innermost edge, as well as its density structure within this region. Results: The average stellar density is found to be on average of $< 10^{-4}$ g cm$^{-3}$ per cubic parsec (pc), with the largest variations being associated with the inner part of GC1, where the density has been as high as around $> 2 \times 10^{-5} g cm^{-3}$. Conclusions: Our analysis demonstrates that GC1 exhibits clear signatures of high-star formation activity, such as higher surface temperatures along with more abundant gas in the central region compared to the outer parts of the star cluster. This finding suggests that GC1 is likely to contain substantial amounts of young stars or even active galaxies, possibly indicating the existence of significant amounts of low mass stars or dark matter halos near the center. Furthermore, our work provides a first-ever measurement of stellar density and abundance in the dense central region of a giant molecular cloud, offering valuable insights into the physical properties of this cosmic dust bowl. This research has broad implications for understanding stellar formation processes in the interstellar medium and can potentially contribute towards future studies of large-scale structures in the universe.
title: The star-forming content of the W3 giant molecular cloud

text: Title: The Gemini Deep Planet Survey: A New Frontier in Search of Exoplanet Worlds In recent years, the Gemini Deep Planet Survey (GDPS) has significantly expanded our understanding of exoplanets and the properties of their atmospheres through its extensive search across hundreds of star systems. This research project aims to unveil planets that orbit other stars within 15 light-years, challenging traditional views of planetary habitability and providing unique insights into the conditions essential for liquid water on planetary surfaces. GDPS employs high-resolution imaging instruments on the ground-based Gemini telescope to capture detailed images of the distant celestial objects. By leveraging multi-object spectroscopy and high-quality photometry, the project collects data from over 260 individual stars, enabling scientists to study the compositions, physical characteristics, and surface features of various types of exoplanet candidates. The survey covers a wide range of stellar classifications including K-type main-sequence stars, G-type giants, and M-type dwarfs, thereby broadening the horizon of exoplanet discovery. One of the key findings is the discovery of a previously undetected transiting exoplanet planet around the Kepler-44b system, which provides crucial insights into the nature of transits observed by other transit missions like TESS. Transiting exoplanets occur when an exoplanet passes directly between its host star and Earth, capturing the star's gravitational pull but not blocking it entirely. These observations help astronomers understand how transiting planets can affect the behavior of nearby stars, potentially influencing their luminosity and possibly hinting at potential conditions on exoplanet surfaces. Another highlight includes the identification of several low-mass dwarf planets discovered beyond Neptune in the Kuiper Belt, offering valuable data for studies in planetary systems and the dynamics of gas giant moons around these exoplanets. The presence of multiple small bodies such as the recently found Pluto-like object Borei suggests the existence of larger icy bodies that may retain substantial amounts of water, further expanding astrobiology possibilities related to habitable environments on other worlds. The GDPS collaboration continues to expand our knowledge base on the composition, structure, and atmospheres of exoplanets. By monitoring these distant systems continuously, researchers hope to uncover new clues about the fundamental aspects of planetary formation and evolution, contributing to our comprehensive picture of the exoplanetary system. Acknowledgments: We gratefully acknowledge support from the National Science Foundation, NASA, and the U.S. Department of Energy for funding this ambitious research project. Without these grants, this research would not have been possible, thus enhancing our capability in the field of exoplanet science. --- This abstract summarizes the primary objectives, methodologies, achievements, and implications of the Gemini Deep Planet Survey project, focusing on its role in the field of exoplanet detection and characterization.
title: The Gemini Deep Planet Survey -- GDPS

text: A jet or relativistic jet is a stream of gas that moves at speeds exceeding the speed of light and often has an apparent direction opposite to its actual motion. Jet-breaks occur when such streams form part of the shock front of a black hole and cause the jet to be deflected or disrupted, leading to changes in the afterglow's x-ray light curves. These effects can impact various astronomical phenomena, including the behavior of celestial bodies like stars and their planets. The study of jets during the afterglow phase of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) provides valuable insights into these processes and helps us understand how different types of energy release mechanisms work in extreme astrophysical environments. By examining the x-ray light curves of GRBs' afterglows, we aim to identify patterns related to jet-mass ratios in the ejecta, allowing scientists to deduce information about the physical properties of the central black hole as well as the conditions under which this process occurs. This research aims to contribute to the understanding of relativistic jet physics and their potential applications beyond GRBs. It also highlights the importance of studying relativistic jets both within and outside the context of GRBs, providing a broader perspective on the fundamental processes taking place in the universe.
title: Jet-breaks in the X-ray Light-Curves of Swift GRB Afterglows

text: In this study, we analyze the precision and feasibility of celestial poles observations across the free core nutation frequency (FCN) band using modern laser interferometric techniques. The main objective is to identify the best frequency band for precise observation and establish the necessary calibration standards required for accurate measurements. Additionally, the analysis involves investigating the effects of noise sources such as atmospheric turbulence on the accuracy of these observations. This research provides valuable insights into the technical challenges involved in observing high-frequency celestial movements and highlights the need for advanced computational methods to address the limitations presented by current hardware capabilities.
title: An analysis of celestial pole offset observations in the free core nutation frequency band

text: This research explores the dynamics of size-selected gold nanoparticles using ultrafast electron nanocrystallography to study their structural evolution and interaction with their environment. By employing pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE), we observed that particles selected by size have distinct morphological characteristics before and after fragmentation into smaller sizes. This study highlights the significant impact of particle size on the nanoparticle's properties in terms of morphology and surface chemistry, providing valuable insights into the formation mechanisms of complex structures formed during particle fragmentation. The ultrafast techniques allow for detailed visualization of these changes, enabling researchers to understand how different particle sizes influence the outcomes of nanoparticle processes such as aggregation, dissolution, and phase transformation.
title: Dynamics of Size-Selected Gold Nanoparticles Studied by Ultrafast Electron Nanocrystallography

text: The paper presents an analysis of topological properties that indicate the potential for detecting non-trivial topologies in a network. The authors explore various metrics and techniques to quantify these characteristics, aiming to provide insights into how they might help identify potentially complex or unpredictable networks. The study utilizes clustering algorithms to group similar topological features together, thereby facilitating the detection process. By examining patterns at different hierarchical levels (i.e., individual nodes, edges, bridges), the methodology offers a comprehensive approach to identifying and understanding the underlying topological structures within networks. The findings highlight both strengths and limitations of using these analytical tools to unveil such intricacies, guiding researchers in developing more robust strategies for network analysis.
title: On the detectability of non-trivial topologies

text: This study presents a detailed exploration into the model-independent constraints on Delta F = 2 (DFF) operators within the Standard Model (SM). It delves into the role these operators play in various particle physics contexts, particularly focusing on their impact on theoretical predictions for new physics scenarios. The researchers systematically investigate the implications of DFFs through the lens of experimental data and theoretical frameworks, aiming to provide insights that challenge current theories regarding the structure of subatomic particles. By analyzing vast datasets ranging from high-energy colliders such as LHC and accelerator experiments like Large Hadron Collider (LHC), this work highlights significant discrepancies between observed data and theoretical expectations associated with DFFs. These discrepancies indicate potential inconsistencies or lack thereof concerning the underlying mechanisms responsible for these interactions, suggesting avenues for future investigations and potential improvements in model selection methods or parameter tuning processes. Furthermore, the study underscores the limitations inherent in directly measuring DFFs with existing theoretical tools, emphasizing the need for more direct experimental approaches to fully understand how DFFs contribute to the SM and beyond. The research contributes to the broader field of model-independent constraints, encouraging further exploration into the nuances governing the behavior of DFF operators across different physical regimes. By addressing key questions related to the consistency of SM models against observed experiments, this work promises valuable contributions to both particle physics and theoretical cosmology.
title: Model-independent constraints on Delta F=2 operators and the scale of New Physics

text: A comprehensive study on turbulent mixing in the surface layers of accreting neutron stars aims to advance our understanding of these celestial objects in their central regions. The research focuses on examining the complex physical phenomena occurring near the neutron star's inner boundaries due to the gravitational effects exerted by its massive density and rotation. The methodology employed involves high-resolution imaging observations using X-ray telescopes at ground-based sites to capture detailed images from the dense core region beneath the neutron star. This allows for the measurement of large-scale turbulence as it propagates into the outer layer of the accretion disc through both thermal convection and shear flows. Results highlight that turbulent mixing is highly active near the neutron star's inner boundary, with notable signatures observable in both X-ray emissions and temperature fluctuations across different frequency bands. This study underscores the critical role of turbulence in shaping the evolution of accreting neutron stars beyond their outer surfaces, contributing significantly to our comprehension of extreme astronomical conditions. This work represents an important step towards unraveling the mechanisms governing the dynamics within the stellar interior and has broad implications for our understanding of stellar structure and evolution, particularly for neutron stars.
title: Turbulent Mixing in the Surface Layers of Accreting Neutron Stars

text: Perverse coherent sheaves and the Geometry of Special Pieces in the Unipotent Variety This paper focuses on a study of perverse coherent sheaves on the unipotent variety over an algebraic closure of $\mathbb{C}$, which generalizes to arbitrary commutative rings $R$ and their maximal ideals $\mathfrak{m}$. The authors investigate the relationship between perverse cohomology with respect to a given module $M$, called $\textbf{Co}_\bullet(M)$, and the dimension of the corresponding spaces, denoted by $\mathrm{dim}\textbf{Co}_\bullet(M)$. Specifically, they explore conditions under which $\textbf{Co}_\bullet(M)$ is supported at a single point or on certain open manifolds, leading to various interpretations including geometric properties like singularities, moduli space structure, and stability criteria for sheaves. The main finding is that for $\textbf{Co}_\bullet(M)$ to be supported at one point, it must be coherent at that point, implying a specific positivity condition involving the Frobenius lift of elements in $M$. They also show that if $\mathrm{dim}\textbf{Co}_\bullet(M)=0$, then $\textbf{Co}_\bullet(M)$ can be described as "special" by a particular filtration. This provides insights into the geometric interpretation of cohomological information captured by the sheaf's stalks. Additionally, the researchers extend this analysis beyond $\mathbb{Z}/p^\infty$, showing how these techniques connect with other aspects such as the theory of non-commutative projective spaces and motivic decomposition schemes. Overall, the study offers new perspectives on the topological and geometrical properties of perverse coherent sheaves, bridging algebraic and arithmetic concepts.
title: Perverse coherent sheaves and the geometry of special pieces in the unipotent variety

text: The paper discusses the study of interacting electrons in Graphene (graph), under the Renormalized Ring-Diagram approximation. The interaction term is defined as an attractive Coulomb interaction between pairs of electrons within the ring, with a potential energy density that can be calculated using the renormalized Ring-Diagram representation. This framework provides a way to account for electron-electron interactions on very small scales when applying first-principles molecular dynamics simulations. The paper introduces new tools and methods to investigate the behavior of interacting electrons in Graphene, offering insights into fundamental electronic properties such as charge carrier distribution and electronic transport properties. These findings have potential implications for understanding the behavior of electrons in various materials including Graphene-based systems, where interlayer couplings play a crucial role in electron transport and energy storage.
title: Study of interacting electrons in graphene under the renormalized-ring-diagram approximation

text: In this paper, we present a study on low-lying ultraviolet (UV) corrections to baryon spectra within a non-relativistic constituent quark model (CNQM). By applying the renormalization group (RG) approach in conjunction with various renormalization schemes, including conventional RG, perturbative RG with loop integrals, and effective field theories, we analyze the UV divergences resulting from the strong coupling constant α (λ), color statistics, color force constants g0 and g1, as well as other parameters of the CNQM. We then derive and analyze an explicit UV regulator that ensures the convergence of the renormalized quantities at all orders of the α loop integral for baryons. The analysis reveals the existence of UV anomalies and confirms the correctness of our derivations through detailed calculations. Keywords: baryons, ultraviolet regularization, nonrelativistic constituent quark model, renormalization group approach, UV divergence, renormalization scheme Acknowledgements: This research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under grants No. 12005147 and No. 13203268, and was conducted under the project number 18M5201.
title: Low-lying ud anti-s anti-s configurations in a non-relativistic constituent quark model

text: In this study, we investigate non-markovian entanglement dynamics of quantum continuous-variable (CV) systems embedded within thermal environments. Unlike traditional models that assume instantaneous memory or correlations between system parts based on an exponential decay rate, the present work employs a novel approach involving multiple time-scales to capture different temporal aspects of the dynamics. By considering not just the initial conditions but also the fluctuationally driven evolution of system properties over time, we demonstrate how non-Markovian entanglement can evolve under conditions that exhibit both long-term coherence and short-range correlation. This method offers insights into complex phenomena such as decoherence, noise-induced entanglement breakdown, and phase transitions observed in CV systems under various thermal fluctuations. The findings provide robust experimental frameworks for understanding the interplay between these two fundamental ingredients in quantum physics.
title: Non-Markovian entanglement dynamics of quantum continuous variable systems in thermal environments

text: In recent decades, bulk viscous cosmology has emerged as a framework for explaining dark energy dynamics and other fundamental aspects of the large-scale structure of the universe. This research explores how bulk viscous forces could potentially affect the evolution of the universe, particularly in high-density environments where conventional perturbation theory may be less effective. Utilizing analytical tools from classical mechanics and advanced perturbation techniques, we investigate the effects of mass density perturbations on the linear growth rate of matter power spectrum and on the amplitude of curvature fluctuations. Our findings suggest that bulk viscous forces play a crucial role in shaping the cosmic microwave background and accelerating power spectra, providing evidence for the existence of dark energy or dark radiation in the early universe. However, our analysis also highlights potential complications such as degeneracies and additional sources of non-linear terms within bulk viscous models. By addressing these issues, this paper advances our understanding of bulk viscous cosmological scenarios and expands the scope of theoretical studies into new regions of the universe's physical space.
title: Bulk Viscous Cosmology

text: The goal was to develop an algorithm that combines sequential decision-making and scanning techniques for analyzing multi-dimensional data sets. The motivating idea is that many complex datasets have multiple dimensions, and the traditional sequential approach (i.e., waiting for individual dimensions before moving on) can be inefficient or misleading. In this study, we proposed an algorithm called the "Scanning Sequence" framework. This framework uses both sequential decision-making (such as using rules) and scanning strategies to efficiently analyze large, unstructured multi-dimensional databases. The core innovation lies in integrating these two approaches into a single, cohesive framework. To evaluate our algorithm's performance, we conducted extensive experiments with both synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing it against existing state-of-the-art techniques. Our main findings include: 1. Comprehensive Approach: Our algorithm combines sequential decisions and scanning operations, making it more efficient in handling multiple-dimensional input. 2. Performance Improvement: Experimental results show that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods in several important evaluation metrics. 3. Economic Performance: By combining sequential decisions with scanning, the algorithm offers competitive economic efficiency compared to purely sequential approaches. 4. Applications: The algorithm has been successfully applied across various domains such as pattern recognition, machine learning, and data mining. By providing a comprehensive solution that leverages both sequential and scanning capabilities, our work demonstrates the practical application of advanced algorithms in handling high-dimensional and noisy data. Our findings have significant implications for improving data analysis, reducing computational time, and enhancing decision-making processes in diverse fields like science, engineering, finance, and healthcare.
title: Scanning and Sequential Decision Making for Multi-Dimensional Data - Part II: the Noisy Case

text: The study explores the potential for achieving a scenario referred to as a 'sudden future singularity' or an anticipated collapse into the null event horizon. It investigates how quickly this concept can be reached given the current state of space and time, focusing on the implications for both technology and societal development. The investigation reveals that while the speed at which such scenarios may come true remains uncertain, the magnitude of their impact in accelerating our technological capabilities has become increasingly plausible within scientific and theoretical frameworks. Additionally, the analysis considers the ethical and societal ramifications of these early outcomes, offering insights into what might be required to achieve a stable future. The paper concludes by suggesting that understanding the juncture between quantum mechanics and general relativity could be crucial to predict the onset and trajectory of these singular events, thereby facilitating strategic planning and decision-making processes in the context of rapidly approaching the end-of-history epoch described by Susskind's theories of accelerated life.
title: How far is it to a sudden future singularity of pressure?

text: The paper discusses the superfluid phase of trapped fermions on a periodic lattice, including the formation of an imbalance between particle and anti-particle flavors at the crossover from the baryon to chiral phases. A BCS-BEC crossover is proposed as the transition point between these two phases, leading to a superconducting and Bose-Einstein condensate state coexisting on different regions of the lattice. The paper then analyzes numerical simulations conducted using the finite temperature renormalized field theory approach within mean field approximation, employing three different quantum phase approximations: T-matrix functional renormalization group, exact diagonalizability approximation, and a combination of both. These methods yield insights into the properties of this imbalanced phase such as fluctuations in the density matrix, correlations between particles and anti-particles, and their implications on transport coefficients, magnetic properties, and quantum mechanical effects within the crossover region. The results suggest that while the superfluid order remains dominant, there can be enhanced phonon excitation rates along some sublattice lines at the crossover boundary. The analysis also indicates how the balance of interactions across the lattice affects the overall behavior and predictions of the model. This work provides foundational insights into understanding the superfluid phase dynamics in confined Fermi systems and has potential applications in condensed matter physics, material science, and beyond.
title: Imbalanced Superfluid Phase of a Trapped Fermi Gas in the BCS-BEC Crossover Regime

text: This study examines the dust covering factor (DCF) that influences stellar winds and their impact on the formation and evolution of luminous quasar (QSO). The authors investigate three key factors: the amount and distribution of dust covering different regions of the QSO's host galaxy, the properties of silicate grains within dust grains, and the contribution of silicates to stellar winds. The DCF is determined through multi-wavelength optical spectroscopy, X-ray spectroscopy, and high-resolution interferometry. It reveals how various aspects of cosmic environments significantly influence QSO emission, particularly when compared with nearby radio-mono-energetic quasars at similar distances from Earth. The results provide a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between dust concentration, wind dynamics, and star formation processes in QSO environments. Key findings include: 1. Effect of Dust on Stellar Winds: A reduction in DCF leads to an increase in the mass fraction of solar wind particles escaping onto quasar envelopes. 2. Silicate Dynamics: Silicification increases the effective temperature of grains within dust aggregates, influencing gas-phase ionization rates and thereby altering the wind's speed profile. 3. Star Formation Efficiency: As a consequence, more silicates contribute to stellar winds, potentially enhancing the ability of QSO cores to form massive stars and generate outflows. 4. Impact on Quasar Emission: Higher levels of silicates can enhance the obscuration around QSO emission features, thus affecting both its intrinsic luminosity and its observed spectrum. These insights have significant implications for our understanding of stellar feedback mechanisms, galaxy interactions, and the chemical composition of the universe's birthplaces. By quantifying the role of dust and silicates, researchers can gain deeper insights into the formation and evolution of QSOs, providing crucial data for future studies of extreme stellar environments and the structure of galactic cosmic rays.
title: Dust covering factor, silicate emission and star formation in luminous QSOs

text: In quantum mechanics, single photons (a form of electromagnetic radiation) represent the smallest indivisible unit, with no associated energy content beyond their individual momentum and frequency being measurable. The use of such light as fundamental resources in quantum systems has significant practical implications, especially for advanced cryptographic applications. Single-photon sources serve crucially to generate these resources efficiently and reliably. This study proposes a novel mathematical criterion based on a specific property observed during single photon generation from nonlinear optical solitons to ensure that the generated single photons exhibit coherent behavior, thereby enhancing the security of quantum-key distribution (QKD) protocols. Through rigorous theoretical analysis, the criteria can be validated against both ideal models and experimental outcomes. The proposed approach not only clarifies how quantum information can be encoded using coherent states but also opens pathways towards more secure quantum communication channels. Therefore, this research contributes significantly to advancing our understanding of quantum systems and their role in modern technological advancements.
title: A mathematical criterion for single photon sources used in quantum cryptography

text: This research aims to develop rate adaptation mechanisms for cognitive radio systems that operate in the spectrum with primary users, incorporating an interference penalty mechanism to maintain system performance amidst varying channel conditions and resource allocation constraints. The study explores how different adaptive strategies can be incorporated within the cognitive radio protocol architecture to optimize spectral efficiency while minimizing interference between secondary users. Utilizing statistical signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) metrics across channels and user group classification methods, this approach assesses how to distribute the available resources among various tasks efficiently and effectively, thereby enhancing overall system resilience against variations in network usage environments. This innovative method promises to mitigate the impact of increasing user demands on cognitive radio networks, particularly for scenarios where there is significant demand for bandwidth at the moment when users have less congestion. By leveraging computational optimization techniques and advanced data analytics, this research aims to enhance the capacity and reliability of these systems.
title: Rate Adaptation for Cognitive Radio under Interference from Primary Spectrum User
